summary: Defines a YANG data model with a factory-reset RPC to reset a server to its factory default condition, plus an optional factory-default datastore for reading the default configuration. It conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: A reset button for network gear, plus a way to peek at what the original settings were.

questions: how to factory reset a device with netconf
does factory reset securely erase keys
what yang module defines factory reset
subtitle: A standard way to reset a network device to factory defaults, and optionally to read what those defaults are.

tldr.problem: When a device's configuration has major errors, restarting configuration from scratch is the best option, but there was no standard way to ask a server to do that.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG module defines a factory-reset RPC that resets the configuration datastores to the contents of a read-only factory-default datastore and restores nonvolatile storage to factory condition.
tldr.outcome: Clients can reset devices in one standard operation, but the device may become unreachable and wiping is not guaranteed to be forensically thorough.

today: RFC 8808 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8342, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8808 defines a YANG data model and mechanism to reset a server to its factory default contents. One example use is when the existing configuration has major errors and starting over is the best option.

It has two parts. The factory-reset remote procedure call (RPC) replaces all previous configuration settings with the factory default contents. An optional read-only factory-default datastore holds the data used for that replacement and can also be read with the <get-data> operation. The model conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture in RFC 8342, and this RFC updates RFC 8342.
sections.plainLanguage: If a gadget's settings get badly messed up, you can wipe them back to how it came from the factory. You can also peek at what those original settings were.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC reuses terms from RFC 8342 and RFC 7950 without redefining them, including the running, startup, candidate, intended and operational datastores and the conventional configuration datastore.

It defines one term: the factory-default datastore, a read-only configuration datastore holding a preset initial configuration that is used to initialize the configuration of a server. It is referred to as <factory-default>.
sections.plainLanguage: Most words come from earlier documents. The one new idea is a locked box that holds the original settings.

sections.title: The Factory-Reset RPC
sections.content:
On receiving factory-reset, all supported conventional read-write configuration datastores (<running>, <startup> and <candidate>) are reset to the contents of <factory-default>. Read-only datastores get their contents from other datastores, for example <intended> from <running>. All data in any dynamic configuration datastores MUST be discarded, and <operational> MUST reflect the state after the defaults are applied.

The RPC MUST also restore nonvolatile storage to factory condition. Depending on the system this may mean deleting dynamically generated files such as keys, certificates, logs and temporary files. Cryptographic keys that are part of the factory-installed image are retained, such as an Initial Device Identifier (IDevID) certificate. For security-sensitive data it is RECOMMENDED to delete as thoroughly as possible, for example by overwriting the storage with zeros and/or random bits. The RPC MAY also trigger other tasks such as restarting the node or some software processes.

Because all read-write datastores are reset at once, the device may become unreachable on the network. Implementors SHOULD reboot the device and get it properly configured, or otherwise restart the processes needed to bootstrap it.
sections.plainLanguage: Pressing reset puts every settings list back to the original and cleans up files the device made itself. Afterward the device may need a restart, and you might not be able to reach it for a while.

sections.title: The Factory-Default Datastore
sections.content:
Following Appendix A of RFC 8342, the RFC defines an optional datastore named factory-default. A device MAY implement the RPC without the datastore, which only removes the ability to programmatically learn the factory default configuration.

  • Schema: either the same as the conventional configuration datastores or a subset of it.
  • Nodes: all config true data nodes.
  • Contents: set by the server in an implementation-dependent manner, and not changeable through NETCONF, RESTCONF, the CLI and so on unless specialized operations exist. They can be read with standard NETCONF or RESTCONF operations.
  • Origin: no new origin identity, because it does not interact with <operational>.

The contents are defined by the device vendor and MUST persist across restarts. If supported, the datastore MUST be listed in the YANG library (RFC 8525).
sections.plainLanguage: The original settings are kept in a read-only copy. You can look at it, but only the maker decides what is in it.

sections.title: The YANG Module
sections.content:
The module is named ietf-factory-default with prefix fd, and its first revision is dated 2020-08-31. It uses YANG version 1.1 and imports the datastore identity from RFC 8342 and the default-deny-all extension from RFC 8341.

It declares a feature factory-default-datastore, an identity factory-default (based on datastore and present only if that feature is supported), and the factory-reset RPC marked with nacm:default-deny-all. The RPC has no input or output parameters in the module.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is a formal description of the reset button and the settings copy, written in a language machines can read.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-factory-default in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant. It also registered the module ietf-factory-default (prefix fd) in the YANG Module Names subregistry, with reference 8808.
sections.plainLanguage: The module's name was written in an official list so nobody else uses it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241, with SSH as the mandatory-to-implement secure transport) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040, with TLS). The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations.

Access to the factory-reset RPC and to the factory default values is considered sensitive, so both are restricted with default-deny-all.

The reset can prevent any further management of the device, for example if session and client configuration is part of the defaults or is overwritten as dynamic files. Storage is expected to be wiped, but there is no guarantee it follows any particular data-cleansing standard. The owner MUST NOT rely on sensitive data such as private keys being forensically unrecoverable afterward.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should get to press reset by default. After a reset you might lock yourself out, and secret files might still be recoverable by experts.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: The running, startup and candidate datastores are reset to the factory-default contents.

items.title: Dynamic data
items.text: All data in dynamic configuration datastores MUST be discarded.

items.title: Operational state
items.text: The operational datastore reflects the state after the defaults apply.

items.title: Storage
items.text: Nonvolatile storage MUST be restored to factory condition.
